system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-02-11 15:44:00 to 2187-02-17 14:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma on surveillance and a history of recurrent cholangitis due to multidrug-resistant E. coli, was admitted with fever and nausea. He had recently completed a four-week course of IV antibiotics for a hepatic abscess but had inadvertently stopped apixaban and ursodiol. On admission, he was restarted on ceftazidime-avibactam and metronidazole. MRI revealed new subcentimeter liver microabscesses. A multidisciplinary team decided to place a percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain to improve biliary drainage and prevent recurrence. A PICC line was placed for IV antibiotic administration. He was discharged home on a four-week course of IV and oral antibiotics, with plans for follow-up MRI and clinic visit. His portal vein thrombosis was managed with apixaban, and iron deficiency anemia was addressed with IV iron infusions.
problems: Unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli] as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other organs and systems
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ cholangioCA w/ h/o MDR E. Coli bacteremia ___ hepatic
microabscesses s/p PTBD ___ presents with fevers despite home Abx. No biliary
output for days per pt. VSS.LFTs baseline. No RUQ pain. consult re: drain
malposition.// PTBD check/reposition/exchange

COMPARISON:  CT scan of the abdomen dated ___, PTB D placement
dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ Interventional ___ and Dr.
___, Interventional Radiology fellow performed the procedure. Dr.
___ supervised the trainee during any key components of the
procedure where applicable and reviewed and agrees with the findings as
reported below.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
50mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 5 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: 1 g ceftriaxone
CONTRAST: 10 ml of Optiray contrast
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 2.3 minutes, 17 mGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Cholangiogram through existing right percutaneous transhepatic biliary
drainage access.
2. Exchange of the existing right percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
catheter with a new 12 ___ PTBD catheter.
PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient. The patient
was then brought to the angiography suite and placed prone on the exam table.
A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol.

The site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  Maximal barrier
technique including hand hygiene, eye wear protection, gloves, sterile gown,
blue drape, face mask and head cap were utilized.  Contrast was injected
through the indwelling tube.  The tube was cut, stay sutures were released and
___ wire was advanced into the small bowel through the tube.  A new 12
___ biliary drain was destrung, flushed and advanced over the wire.  The
wire and inner dilator were removed, the pigtail was partially formed in the
duodenum.  Contrast was injected confirming appropriate positioning.  The
catheter was sutured to the skin and secured with a StatLock.  Sterile
dressing was applied.  The drain was connected to a bag.  The patient
tolerated the procedure without any complications.

FINDINGS:


1. Cholangiogram through the indwelling drain demonstrates opacification of
some of the right and left intrahepatic biliary ducts with spillage of
contrast from the drain in the hilum into the metallic stents of the common
bile duct to flow into the small bowel.  The does not appear to be direct
passage of contrast through the indwelling drain from the hilum to the
small-bowel.
2. Cholangiogram through the new tube demonstrates passage of contrast through
the drain into the small bowel without opacification of intrahepatic biliary
ducts or spillage into the metallic stents.

IMPRESSION:


1. Successful exchange and upsize of right percutaneous transhepatic biliary
drain from a 10 ___ to a 12 ___ drain.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with new R PICC// 49 cm R basilic SL PICC- ___
___   Contact name: ___: ___

COMPARISON:  Radiographs from ___

IMPRESSION: 

There has been removal of the left-sided PICC line.  There is a new
right-sided PICC line with distal tip in the distal SVC, appropriately sited. 
There is subsegmental atelectasis at both lung bases.  There is no overt
pulmonary edema.  Calcified granuloma within the right mid lung field is again
seen.  There are no pneumothoraces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I see you came in with fevers after your iron infusion. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I was just leaving the infusion center when I started feeling chills and fever. I spiked up to 102, and I knew something was off again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any pain, nausea, or changes in your drain output?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No belly pain, but my PTBD hasn’t been draining much the last few days. I thought maybe it was clogged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely be the issue. We’ve checked your labs and blood cultures, and we found E. coli in your blood. It’s the same multidrug-resistant strain you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no, not again. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but we caught it early. The infection likely came from your biliary system because the drain wasn’t draining well. We’re starting antibiotics right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been taking my home antibiotics every day, so I didn’t think this would happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done everything right. Sometimes the drain gets blocked, and bacteria can grow. We’re giving you ceftazidime-avibactam and metronidazole for now. Infectious disease wants to add two more antibiotics—tobramycin and tigecycline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two more? That’s a lot. Are they safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They are, but we’re monitoring your kidney function closely. We’ll adjust based on your blood culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And what about my drain? Should it be checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to have interventional radiology look at it. A CT scan shows your liver abscesses are stable or even improving, but your drain might be clogged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want to get this under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your repeat blood cultures are negative today, which is a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. I’m feeling a bit better—fever’s gone down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re still waiting for the full sensitivity report, but we’ll likely switch your antibiotics soon to something easier to take at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll place a new one. The old one was removed in the ER, but we need reliable IV access for antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I hope this one lasts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, we’re about to take you for a procedure to exchange your PTBD catheter. It’s likely clogged, and we’ll put in a larger one to improve drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation, so you’ll be comfortable. The team will use imaging to guide the new tube in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They upsized your drain from 10 to 12 French. It’s now draining bile properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I could already see it started draining more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that should help clear the infection. Your blood cultures now confirm the E. coli is sensitive to meropenem, so we’re switching from ceftazidime-avibactam to meropenem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s more targeted. We’re keeping tigecycline because some strains like yours can resist even strong antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is improving, and your liver enzymes are stable. Anemia and platelets are still low, but that’s expected with infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel a bit tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. You also just had two iron infusions recently, so your body is catching up. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my cancer? Is it still stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last scans showed no evidence of disease progression. You’re still on surveillance every six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a new PICC line in your right arm. The X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot in the superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I go home with this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. You’ll get your antibiotics through it. We’re planning to switch meropenem to ertapenem for easier home use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tigecycline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue that too, twice a day. We’ll reassess the duration at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday, you had a small amount of blood come out of your drain when you lifted a table. It stopped quickly, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a brief red flush, then it went back to yellow. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from minor trauma when you strained. Since it resolved and your liver enzymes didn’t rise, we think it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a trial of capping your drain yesterday. You didn’t get any fever or liver enzyme changes, so we’ll discharge you with it capped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need to carry the bag anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. But you’ll need routine exchanges every few months to prevent clogging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today with capped PTBD and your PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have weekly labs sent to the clinic—CBC, liver tests, kidney function. And an MRI of the liver in a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get ertapenem once daily and tigecycline twice daily through the PICC. The infectious disease team will decide how long based on your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my apixaban for the blood clot in the liver vein?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that. The clot is improving, but we need to keep preventing new clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call us if you develop fever, pain, or any issues with the drain or PICC. You’re doing well—keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your iron studies came back. Ferritin is 198, so your stores are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel less fatigued than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep taking your folic acid and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too, Mr. Johnson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, avoid heavy lifting for now to prevent strain on the drain site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma and a history of recurrent cholangitis due to multidrug-resistant E. coli, was admitted with fevers and decreased output from his percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain (PTBD) following an iron infusion. Blood cultures confirmed MDR E. coli bacteremia, and imaging showed stable liver microabscesses with a clogged PTBD. He underwent PTBD exchange with upsizing of the catheter to improve drainage. Initial treatment with ceftazidime-avibactam, metronidazole, and planned tobramycin and tigecycline was adjusted when cultures showed sensitivity to meropenem; he was transitioned to meropenem and tigecycline, later changed to ertapenem for outpatient administration. A new PICC line was placed for IV antibiotics. He had a brief episode of bloody PTBD output after straining, which resolved spontaneously. He tolerated a PTBD capping trial and was discharged home with capped drain, on IV ertapenem and tigecycline, with plans for weekly labs, follow-up MRI, and infectious disease evaluation to determine treatment duration.
